label: Chapter 2: Dukes, Guilds and the Grand Place, 1100 to 1430

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So in the twelfth century, Brussels falls into the hands of an ambitious family.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The counts of Leuven, who held Brussels, steadily rose in rank.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: They became dukes of Lower Lotharingia, and then, as the old title lost its meaning, dukes of Brabant.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And Brabant was a big deal.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: One of the richest territories in northwest Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It stretched across the heart of what is now Belgium and part of the southern Netherlands, and it included great towns like Leuven, Antwerp, and Brussels.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For a long time, Leuven was the leading city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But gradually the dukes spent more time in Brussels, in a castle on a hill called the Coudenberg, which means cold hill.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Cold hill. I like that.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: By the late Middle Ages, Brussels was the main seat of the dukes, and with the dukes came money, officials, and prestige.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: But the dukes weren't the only reason it grew.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: No, Brussels owed its growth just as much to its own people.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The town made cloth. Wool came in from England, weavers and dyers worked it into fabric, and merchants sold it across Europe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Alongside that grew many other crafts: brewing, baking, butchery, metalwork, carpentry, and eventually luxury goods like tapestries.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the people who did those jobs organized themselves.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Into guilds. Part trade union, part business association, part social club, and part political party.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So where does the Grand Place come in?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: At the center of it all was the market.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Down in the valley, on low ground close to the river, there was an open space known as the Lower Market.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Traders set up stalls and townspeople met to do business.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Over the centuries, wooden stalls turned into stone halls, and the guilds built meeting houses around the edges.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So the Grand Place began as a muddy field.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It did. By the end of the thirteenth century, the drapers' guild had its own hall there, and the foundation of the square's future was laid.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Who actually ran the town?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A narrow elite. Power lay in the hands of a few wealthy families, known as the Seven Lineages of Brussels, who held the city council and the best offices.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Below them were the guilds, which had economic muscle but little say in government.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Which sounds like a recipe for trouble.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And over time it boiled over. But first we meet one of the great documents of Brussels history.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1355, the Duke of Brabant, John the Third, died without a male heir.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: His eldest daughter, Joanna, became duchess, and her husband was a man listeners of our Luxembourg episode will remember, Wenceslas of Luxembourg, the half brother of the Emperor Charles the Fourth.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Small world.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In January of 1356, before they could take up their rule, Joanna and Wenceslas had to sign a charter promising to respect the rights of the towns and nobles of Brabant.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's called the Joyous Entry, named for the ceremonial entry a new ruler made into the cities of the duchy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: What did it say?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It limited the power of the duke.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: He couldn't declare war, sign treaties, or raise taxes without the consent of the estates, and it even included a remarkable clause allowing the people of Brabant to withdraw their obedience if the duke broke the rules.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That sounds like the Magna Carta.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It's often compared to it. Historians caution that its later reputation was somewhat exaggerated by romantic writers of the nineteenth century, but it remained an important symbol for centuries, and Brabantine rulers swore to uphold it for generations.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And I gather it was tested almost straight away.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Immediately. Louis of Male, the Count of Flanders, a powerful neighbor with his own claim to Brabant, invaded and seized Brussels in 1356.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: But he didn't hold it for long.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: A citizen named Everard t'Serclaes, from one of the great families, led a night raid with a small band of men, slipped into the city, and drove out the Flemish garrison.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: A folk hero.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Absolutely. He was killed by a rival lord a few decades later, and today a bronze monument to him lies against a wall just off the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: According to local custom, rubbing the bronze arm of the statue brings good luck.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And you can see it's polished bright by the hands of passersby.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: You can. Now, the liberation helped fuel another great project.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: With the city growing quickly, the old walls had become too small.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Between 1356 and 1383, the people of Brussels built a second, much larger ring of walls, with seven main gates and dozens of towers.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: That's a huge undertaking for a town that size.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It enclosed about eight kilometers of ground.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Most of it was torn down in the nineteenth century, and its path is now traced by a ring of boulevards around the old center, known as the Petite Ceinture, or the small ring.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So if I look at a map of central Brussels, that five-sided shape of boulevards is the medieval city?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Exactly. And one gate survives, the heavy, castle-like Porte de Hal, on the southern side of the ring.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Now the Town Hall. That's from this period too.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The early fifteenth century was the great age of civic building.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1402, work began on the Brussels Town Hall, on the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The left wing was built first, and the right wing followed in the fourteen-forties.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1449 the architects began the soaring tower, a lace of stone rising about ninety-six meters, topped by a gilded statue of Saint Michael slaying the dragon.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And there's a famous quirk.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The tower isn't centered above the main doorway, and the wings are of slightly different lengths.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: According to an old story, the architect was so horrified by the asymmetry that he threw himself from the tower.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Oh dear.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Historians think that's just a legend, but it's a good one.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then there's the smallest landmark in the city.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The Manneken Pis. A fountain figure of a little boy relieving himself into a basin, first mentioned in a document from 1388.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The bronze you can visit today is a copy of a version made in 1619 by the sculptor Jérôme Duquesnoy, and it stands on a street corner a few minutes from the Grand Place.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And he has a wardrobe.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Well over a thousand costumes, changed regularly on special occasions.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Many legends try to explain him.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In one, a small duke of Leuven, hung in a basket from a tree during a battle, urinated on the enemy and inspired his soldiers.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In another, a boy put out a burning fuse and saved the city.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So which is true?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: No one knows the real story, and Brussels doesn't seem to mind.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Meanwhile, the tension between the lineages and the guilds finally blows up.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: In 1421. A group of guildsmen, angry about the patricians' control of the government and rising taxes, stormed the town hall, and several city magistrates were killed.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The duke, John the Fourth, intervened to restore order, but the result was a victory for the craftsmen.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: So what changed?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: From then on, the guilds, organized into nine groups known as the Nations of Brussels, had a formal share of power on the city council.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: For the first time, Brussels had a government in which ordinary working people had a say.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And the ducal family kept changing too.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: It did. Wenceslas died in 1383 without children.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Joanna lived until 1406 and left the duchy to her grandnephew, a son of the powerful Duke of Burgundy.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: From then on, Brabant's rulers were a succession of Burgundian princes, one of whom was killed at the Battle of Agincourt in 1415.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: And then?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: The family line died out. And in 1430, the duchy fell to the most powerful of all of them, Philip the Good, Duke of Burgundy.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: If someone is out walking in Brussels right now, what should they look for?

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: On the Grand Place, look up at the Town Hall tower and notice that it's off-center.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Then walk a few steps to the Rue Charles Buls, just off the square, to find the monument to Everard t'Serclaes.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: And a few streets farther, you'll find the Manneken Pis, surprisingly small, and usually surrounded by a crowd.

units.speaker: Anna
units.text: Next chapter, Brussels becomes the capital of an empire.

units.speaker: Ben
units.text: Quite literally.
